advances: The full-row estimate \(\nu\le C\log(K^2b(p))\) has no absolute constant on the active region when the parity occupancy bound is removed, even for complete, full-dimensional, globally affine supports with injective integral-pair midpoints, connected midpoint incidence, and all reflected rows of cardinality at most three. The same witnesses admit a zero-variance row selection with occupied-count energy uniformly above one. Thus this obstructs the proposed full-row bridge, while the selected-row bridge survives on these examples; it is not a counterexample to the locked actual-depth conjecture.

proof:
The raw weights at the simplex vertices below realize the list appearing in accepted fact e452f6b767c2a35b. All geometric, normalization, activity, and row-selection claims needed here are proved directly. The normalization and full/selected row quantities retain exactly the meanings in 445a9e668ee1a705 and 1067298acf6f67ac.

First consider the base in its original \(r\) coordinates. The convex hull of \(0,2e_1,\ldots,2e_r\) is \(2\Delta_r=\lbrace x\in\mathbb R^r:x_i\ge0,\ \sum_i x_i\le2\rbrace\). Its integer points are exactly the listed set \(A\): a nonnegative integral vector of coordinate sum at most two is zero, a single unit vector, twice a unit vector, or the sum of two distinct unit vectors.

The \(r+1\) vertices \(0,2e_i\) occupy one even parity class. Every \(e_i\) occupies its own parity class, and every \(e_i+e_j\), \(i<j\), occupies its own parity class, with none of these classes coinciding. Thus
\(K_A=1+r+\binom r2=(q^6+q^3+2)/2\), and \(|A|=(r+1)(r+2)/2\). The only unordered distinct same-parity pairs are pairs of vertices. Their midpoints are respectively \(e_i\) for \(\lbrace0,2e_i\rbrace\), and \(e_i+e_j\) for \(\lbrace2e_i,2e_j\rbrace\). These midpoints are all distinct. Therefore the full nontrivial base rows are precisely
$$
R_{e_i}=\lbrace0,e_i,2e_i\rbrace,
\qquad
R_{e_i+e_j}=\lbrace2e_i,e_i+e_j,2e_j\rbrace\quad(i<j),
$$
and all base vertex rows are singleton rows. The incidence graph of these base rows is connected: each \(2e_i\) connects to \(0\) through its \(e_i\) row, and each remaining midpoint belongs to a row joining two such vertices.

We next prove the exact effect of one attachment, including completeness. Suppose a complete finite support \(D\subset\mathbb Z^m\) is the integer census of a convex polytope \(Q\), and a supported point \(v\) has singleton full row. Embed \(D\) at new coordinate zero, and adjoin \((v,-1)\) and \((v,1)\). Let \(Q'\) be their convex hull with \(Q\times\lbrace0\rbrace\). Every point of \(Q'\) has new coordinate between \(-1\) and \(1\). Its slice at new coordinate \(1\) is the single point \((v,1)\), and the slice at \(-1\) is \((v,-1)\). Its slice at zero is exactly \(Q\times\lbrace0\rbrace\): a convex combination at height zero uses equal total coefficients on the two new points, whose old-coordinate average is \(v\in Q\). These are the only possible integer heights. Hence the integer census of \(Q'\) is precisely the old support at height zero and the two new points. If \(Q\) is full-dimensional in \(\mathbb R^m\), then \(Q'\) is full-dimensional in \(\mathbb R^{m+1}\).

The two new points share a parity class with each other and with no old point, because their new coordinate is odd and all old new coordinates are zero. Thus the only new unordered distinct same-parity pair is their pair. Its midpoint is \((v,0)\). Because the old row at \(v\) was singleton, this midpoint was not the midpoint of any old distinct pair, so midpoint injectivity is preserved. The only changed old row is the row at \(v\), which becomes the new triple; both new points have singleton rows. Indeed a noncentral reflected pair about either point at height \(1\) or \(-1\) would require two supported points at that same extreme height, where only that point exists. One occupied parity class and two atoms are added. The new row joins the new points to the old incidence component of \(v\).

Apply this operation successively at \(v_{j-1}\) in the new direction \(f_j\), for \(j=1,\ldots,t\). Initially \(v_0=2e_1\) has a singleton row; after step \(j\), the new positive leaf \(v_j\) has a singleton row and is available for the next step. The operation gives exactly the displayed closed forms for \(u_j,v_j\). Induction proves completeness, full dimension \(r+t\), injective midpoints, and connected incidence. It also proves that the complete list of nontrivial rows consists of the base rows and
$$
R_{v_{j-1}}=\lbrace u_j,v_{j-1},v_j\rbrace\quad(1\le j\le t).
$$
Every other row is singleton. The new parity class at step \(j\) remains a two-point class under all later zero-coordinate embeddings. Its added-coordinate parity vector is \((1,\ldots,1,0,\ldots,0)\), with exactly its first \(j\) added coordinates equal to one. These vectors are distinct and nonzero. Consequently the base even class still has exactly \(r+1\) points, every other base class has one point, and the \(t\) new classes have two points each. This proves both the claimed maximum occupancy and
$$
K_s=K_A+t=\frac{3q^6+q^3+2}{2},
\qquad
|D_s|=|A|+2t=\frac{5q^6+3q^3+2}{2}.
$$
All these counts refer to actual occupied parity classes in the stated ambient space.

The raw law is globally affine because
\(\log w_s(x)=3\log q-(\log q)\sum_{i=1}^rx_i\) throughout the entire support. In the base it gives weights \(q^3\) at zero, \(q\) at each \(2e_i\), \(q^2\) at each \(e_i\), and \(q\) at each \(e_i+e_j\). Every added atom has old-coordinate part \(2e_1\), hence weight \(q\). Each attachment therefore has constant weight \(q\) at its two endpoints and its center. In particular \(w_x^2=w_yw_{2x-y}\) on every reflected row, and the same equality holds for the original normalized probabilities. No conditioning or change of law is used.

Let \(Z_A\) be the sum of the base raw weights, \(T_A\) their cube sum, and \(F_A\) their full-row multiplier-weighted cube sum. The exact base counts give
$$
\begin{aligned}
Z_A&=q^3+rq+rq^2+\binom r2q
=\frac{q^7+2q^5+q^4+2q^3}{2},\\
T_A&=q^9+rq^3+rq^6+\binom r2q^3
=\frac{5q^9+q^6}{2},\\
F_A&=q^9+rq^3+9rq^6+9\binom r2q^3
=\frac{29q^9-7q^6}{2}.
\end{aligned}
$$
One attachment adds \(2q\) to the normalizer and \(2q^3\) to the cube sum. Its chosen center had a singleton row and acquires a triple row, so its contribution to the full-row cube sum increases by \((9-1)q^3\); its two new singleton rows contribute another \(2q^3\). Thus each attachment adds exactly \(10q^3\) to that sum. With \(t=q^6\), the resulting totals are
\(Z_s=Z_A+2tq\), \(T_s=T_A+2tq^3\), and \(F_s=F_A+10tq^3\), which are precisely the formulas in the statement. In particular \(Z_s\) is the exact original normalizer of the one affine raw law.

Because each nontrivial row is a triple and affine equality holds, each geometric mean in the row at \(x\) is \(p_s(x)\). Hence \(H_{p_s}(x)=|R_x|p_s(x)\), and the row law \(\kappa_x\) is uniform on its row. Singleton rows have zero variance. In a base row centered at \(e_i\), the score values are \(0,\log q,-\log q\), since its endpoint weights are \(q^3,q\). Therefore its variance is \(2(\log q)^2/3\). Every other nontrivial row has equal endpoint weights and zero score variance: the base rows at \(e_i+e_j\) have endpoint weights \(q,q\), and the attached rows have weight \(q\) everywhere. Thus the exact unnormalized score numerator is
$$
\sum_{x\in D_s}|R_x|^2w_s(x)^3V_x
=r\,9q^6\frac23(\log q)^2
=6q^9(\log q)^2.
$$
The numerator defining \(\nu(p_s)\) is this raw sum divided by \(Z_s^3\), whereas \(b(p_s)=F_s/Z_s^3\). Cancelling this same original normalization gives
$$
\nu(p_s)=\frac{6q^9}{F_s}(\log q)^2
=\frac{12}{49-7q^{-3}}(\log q)^2.
$$

For the finite energy bounds, suppress the subscript \(s\). The exact formulas imply
$$
\begin{aligned}
3Z-5qK&=q(q-1)(3q^3+2q^2+5q+5)\ge0,\\
9q^2Z-5T&=9q^7+2q^6+9q^5>0,\\
49q^2Z-5F&=49q^7+42q^6+49q^5>0.
\end{aligned}
$$
In particular \(K\le3Z/(5q)\), \(T\le9q^2Z/5\), and \(F\le49q^2Z/5\). Substitution yields
$$
A_0=\frac{K^2T}{Z^3}\le\frac{81}{125}<1,
\qquad
A_{\mathcal J}=\frac{K^2F}{Z^3}\le\frac{441}{125}.
$$
This proves activity uniformly for every \(s\ge1\).

For the asserted selection, put \(\widehat R_x=R_x\) at the \(t\) attachment centers \(v_0,\ldots,v_{t-1}\), and \(\widehat R_x=\lbrace x\rbrace\) at every other center. All its nontrivial rows have equal raw weights \(q\), so every selected score is zero, including those in singleton rows. Therefore \(\widehat V_x=0\) at every center and \(\widehat\nu(p_s)=0\). Relative to the atom sum, the \(t\) selected triple centers each add \(8q^3\), giving
$$
\widehat F:=Z^3\widehat b(p_s)=T+8tq^3
=T_A+10tq^3=\frac{25q^9+q^6}{2}.
$$
For \(q\ge2\), the elementary estimates
$$
K\ge\frac32q^6,\qquad
\widehat F\ge\frac{25}{2}q^9,\qquad
\frac{Z}{q^7}
=\frac{5+2q^{-2}+q^{-3}+2q^{-4}}2
\le\frac{23}{8}
$$
show that
$$
K^2\widehat b(p_s)=\frac{K^2\widehat F}{Z^3}
\ge\frac{(3/2)^2(25/2)}{(23/8)^3}
=\frac{14400}{12167}>1.
$$
Every selected row is contained in its full row, so \(\widehat b(p_s)\le b(p_s)\). This proves the claimed lower bound for \(A_{\mathcal J}\) as well and, in particular, makes its logarithm positive.

It remains to verify the limits and the failure of a uniform full-row price. The exact formulas give
$$
\frac K{q^6}\longrightarrow\frac32,\quad
\frac Z{q^7}\longrightarrow\frac52,\quad
\frac T{q^9}\longrightarrow\frac92,\quad
\frac F{q^9}\longrightarrow\frac{49}{2},\quad
\frac{\widehat F}{q^9}\longrightarrow\frac{25}{2}.
$$
Inserting these five limits into the energy ratios yields respectively \(81/125\), \(441/125\), and \(9/5\), and the explicit variance formula gives \(\nu(p_s)/(\log q)^2\to12/49\). More directly, the proved finite bounds imply
$$
\nu(p_s)\ge\frac{12}{49}(\log q)^2,
\qquad
0<\log A_{\mathcal J,s}\le\log\frac{441}{125}.
$$
Given any finite \(C\ge0\), choose an integer \(s\ge1\) with
\(s>\sqrt{49C\log(441/125)/12}/\log2\). Then \(q=2^s\) produces an active complete globally affine law satisfying all the stated geometric restrictions and
\(\nu(p_s)>C\log A_{\mathcal J,s}\). This is a finite counterexample for that constant. The selected energy bound and zero selected price hold simultaneously for this same original law, establishing the stated scope of the obstruction.
statement:
Use the canonical full reflected quantities of accepted facts 445a9e668ee1a705 and 1067298acf6f67ac. Explicitly, for a positive law \(p\) on a finite support \(D\subset\mathbb Z^n\), extended by zero off \(D\), put
$$
\begin{aligned}
R_x&=\lbrace y\in D:2x-y\in D\rbrace,&
H_p(x)&=\sum_{y\in R_x}\sqrt{p_yp_{2x-y}},&
b(p)&=\sum_{x\in D}p_xH_p(x)^2,\\
\kappa_x(y)&=\frac{\sqrt{p_yp_{2x-y}}}{H_p(x)},&
Y_x(y)&=\frac12\log\frac{p_y}{p_{2x-y}},&
V_x&=\mathbb E_{\kappa_x}Y_x^2,\\
\nu(p)&=\frac{\sum_{x\in D}p_xH_p(x)^2V_x}{b(p)}.
\end{aligned}
$$
Here the reflected sum is oriented, including its central term once. Let \(K\) be the number of occupied coordinatewise parity classes of \(D\), exactly as in 1067298acf6f67ac, and put \(A_0=K^2\sum_xp_x^3\) and \(A_{\mathcal J}=K^2b(p)\). In particular \(K\) is not the ambient count \(2^n\).

For every integer \(s\ge1\), set \(q=2^s\), \(r=q^3\), \(t=q^6\), and \(n=r+t\). Write \(e_1,\ldots,e_r,f_1,\ldots,f_t\) for the standard coordinate vectors of \(\mathbb R^n\), and define
$$
\begin{aligned}
A&=\lbrace0\rbrace\cup\lbrace e_i,2e_i:1\le i\le r\rbrace
\cup\lbrace e_i+e_j:1\le i<j\le r\rbrace,\\
v_0&=2e_1,\qquad
v_j=2e_1+\sum_{h=1}^jf_h,\qquad
u_j=2e_1+\sum_{h=1}^{j-1}f_h-f_j\quad(1\le j\le t),\\
D_s&=A\cup\lbrace u_j,v_j:1\le j\le t\rbrace,
\qquad Q_s=\operatorname{conv}(D_s).
\end{aligned}
$$
The support satisfies \(D_s=Q_s\cap\mathbb Z^n\), and \(Q_s\) is full-dimensional. The midpoint map on unordered distinct same-parity pairs is injective, and every such midpoint lies in \(D_s\). The midpoint-incidence graph is connected: here its atom vertices are the points of \(D_s\), its other vertices are the nontrivial reflected rows, and an atom is incident with every row containing it. Its largest parity class has exactly \(r+1\) points.

Give the entire support the single globally affine raw weight law
\(w_s(x)=q^{3-\sum_{i=1}^rx_i}\), and use the original probability law \(p_s(x)=w_s(x)/Z_s\), with
$$
\begin{aligned}
K_s&=\frac{3q^6+q^3+2}{2},&
Z_s&=\sum_{x\in D_s}w_s(x)
=\frac{5q^7+2q^5+q^4+2q^3}{2},\\
T_s&=\sum_{x\in D_s}w_s(x)^3
=\frac{9q^9+q^6}{2},&
F_s&=\sum_{x\in D_s}|R_x|^2w_s(x)^3
=\frac{49q^9-7q^6}{2}.
\end{aligned}
$$
Every nontrivial reflected row has exactly three points, and \(H_{p_s}(x)=|R_x|p_s(x)\). Consequently
$$
\begin{aligned}
A_{0,s}&=\frac{K_s^2T_s}{Z_s^3}\le\frac{81}{125}<1,\\
1&<\frac{14400}{12167}\le A_{\mathcal J,s}
=\frac{K_s^2F_s}{Z_s^3}\le\frac{441}{125},\\
\nu(p_s)&=\frac{12}{49-7q^{-3}}(\log q)^2.
\end{aligned}
$$
In particular no finite absolute \(C\ge0\) can satisfy \(\nu(p)\le C\log(K^2b(p))\) for every complete globally affine law with injective integral-pair midpoints and \(A_0<1\), even with the additional connectedness and three-point-row conditions above.

There is also an explicit surviving row selection. Retain the full triple at each center \(v_0,\ldots,v_{t-1}\) and retain only the central atom at every other center. Define the selected reflected quantities by the same formulas using these symmetric selected rows and the same original law \(p_s\). Then
$$
\widehat\nu(p_s)=0,\qquad
K_s^2\widehat b(p_s)
=\frac{K_s^2(25q^9+q^6)}{2Z_s^3}
\ge\frac{14400}{12167}>1.
$$
The exact limits along \(q=2^s\to\infty\) are
$$
A_{0,s}\longrightarrow\frac{81}{125},\qquad
A_{\mathcal J,s}\longrightarrow\frac{441}{125},\qquad
\frac{\nu(p_s)}{(\log q)^2}\longrightarrow\frac{12}{49},\qquad
K_s^2\widehat b(p_s)\longrightarrow\frac95.
$$
